text: Your child can likely tell simple stories with a beginning, middle, and end. Ask open-ended questions like "What happened next?" to encourage narrative skills.
Your child may start showing interest in writing letters or their name. Let them practice on large paper with thick crayons or markers — scribbles and attempts are all part of learning.
Your child is developing a sense of humor and may love silly jokes and wordplay. Laughing together strengthens your bond and builds language skills.
Skipping, hopping, and galloping show maturing gross motor coordination. Practice these movements through games rather than drills.
Your child may have an imaginary friend. This is healthy and shows advanced cognitive development, creativity, and emotional processing.
Counting to 10 or beyond, recognizing some numbers, and understanding "more" and "less" are typical math skills at this age.
Your child is learning to draw people and may include a head, body, arms, or legs. By their fourth birthday, drawing a person with 3 or more body parts is a common milestone.
Friendships become more meaningful now. Your child may have a preferred friend and start navigating the complexity of social relationships.
Your child understands basic rules and fairness. Use games and family activities to reinforce that rules apply to everyone equally.
Cutting along a line with scissors, buttoning their shirt, and using a zipper all show fine motor skills are maturing. Celebrate the effort.
Your child may mix up fantasy and reality sometimes. Gently help them distinguish between pretend and real without discouraging imagination.
Encourage your child to solve small problems independently before jumping in. "What do you think we should try?" builds confidence and critical thinking.
Your child can likely sort objects by multiple attributes — color AND size, for example. Sorting laundry or toys together makes this fun and practical.
Emotional regulation is still developing. Help your child name complex feelings like "disappointed" or "jealous" — a rich emotional vocabulary helps them cope.
Your child may show interest in letters and early reading. Follow their lead — point out words on signs and let them "read" familiar books to you.
Many children drop their nap between ages 3 and 5, though some still need one. If your child no longer naps, aim for a bedtime early enough to get 10-13 hours of overnight sleep.
Your child may try to negotiate bedtime endlessly. Set a predictable routine and stick to it lovingly — "We read two books, then lights out" provides clarity.
Nightmares can be more vivid at this age as imagination expands. Comfort your child and talk through the dream briefly without dwelling on it.
If your child is afraid of the dark, brainstorm solutions together — a special nightlight, a "brave buddy" stuffed animal, or a quick room check can help.
Quiet time before bed is just as important as the sleep itself. Reading, gentle stretching, or quiet conversation helps the brain transition to rest.
If your child wakes frequently at night, check for environmental causes first — room temperature, noise, light, or an uncomfortable mattress.
A consistent wake time matters as much as a consistent bedtime. Try to keep morning wake-ups within 30 minutes of the same time daily.
Your child may start resisting bedtime by saying they're not tired. A calming routine helps the body wind down even when the mind feels alert.
Bedwetting is completely normal at this age. Use a waterproof mattress protector and avoid making it a big deal — most children outgrow it by 5-6.
If your child has dropped the nap recently, you might notice crankiness in the late afternoon. A brief rest period with a book can help bridge the gap.
Deep breathing exercises before bed can help your child learn to self-soothe. Try "smell the flower, blow out the candle" as a simple technique.
Avoid sugary snacks close to bedtime. If your child needs a pre-bed snack, choose something light like a banana or a small handful of crackers.
Your child may stall by asking for more water or bathroom trips. Allow one pre-bed trip and one small cup of water, then hold the boundary gently.
Sharing a "best part of the day" at bedtime gives your child something positive to think about as they fall asleep and strengthens your connection.
If your child consistently fights bedtime, they may not be tired enough. Ensure they're getting plenty of physical activity during the day.
Your child can use a butter knife to spread soft foods and help cut tender items. These kitchen skills build confidence and fine motor control.
Talk about food in terms of what it does for the body — "Carrots help your eyes" or "Protein makes your muscles strong" — to build food literacy.
If your child refuses an entire food group, find creative alternatives. Won't eat vegetables? Try them in smoothies, muffins, or as part of a dipping plate.
Your child can help with more complex cooking tasks now — stirring batter, cracking eggs with help, or sprinkling toppings. Cooking together builds enthusiasm for eating.
Model the eating habits you want your child to develop. They notice and mimic how you talk about food and what you choose to eat.
Fiber is important for digestion. Offer whole grain bread, oatmeal, berries, and beans regularly to keep things running smoothly.
Teach your child to recognize hunger and fullness signals. "Is your tummy still hungry?" is better than "Finish your plate."
Growing a small herb garden or sprouting seeds teaches your child where food comes from. Kids love eating things they grew themselves.
Try "food bridges" — if your child likes french fries, introduce baked sweet potato fries. Use foods they enjoy as a bridge to similar new foods.
Your child needs about 2 to 2.5 cups of dairy or calcium-equivalent per day. If they don't like milk, yogurt, cheese, and calcium-fortified foods count too.
Mealtimes should last about 20-30 minutes. If your child hasn't eaten after that, calmly end the meal. They'll eat at the next opportunity.
Encourage your child to try one bite of new foods without forcing. Over time, this gentle exposure approach works better than pressure.
Omega-3 fatty acids support brain development. Include fish, walnuts, chia seeds, or flaxseed in your child's diet when possible.
Avoid using food as a comfort or reward. Instead, teach your child other ways to celebrate or feel better — a hug, a game, or time together.
Your child can drink from an open cup skillfully now. Offer water throughout the day and keep sugary drinks as occasional treats.
Your child may be due for important vaccine boosters during this stage. Talk to your pediatrician to make sure immunizations are up to date.
Your child should brush their teeth twice daily with a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste. Help them brush until they can tie their own shoes — around age 6-7.
Vision screening is recommended annually between ages 3 and 5. Catching conditions like amblyopia (lazy eye) early gives treatment the best chance of success.
If your child complains of growing pains in their legs at night, gentle massage and a warm compress usually help. These pains are normal and temporary.
Teach your child to wash their hands properly: wet, lather, scrub for 20 seconds, rinse, dry. This is especially important before meals and after the bathroom.
Your child's first permanent molars will arrive around age 6. When they do, ask your dentist about dental sealants to protect them from cavities.
Your child may start to experience seasonal allergies. A runny nose with clear mucus, sneezing, and itchy eyes that persist are signs worth discussing with your doctor.
Pink eye (conjunctivitis) spreads easily among children. Teach your child not to touch their eyes and to use their own towel.
If your child has asthma, work with your pediatrician on an action plan. Know the difference between daily controller medication and rescue inhalers.
Check your child's posture during activities. A sturdy, child-sized chair and table help prevent slouching during drawing or eating.
Lice are common in group settings and have nothing to do with hygiene. Teach your child not to share hats, brushes, or hair accessories.
Your child can start learning to blow their nose effectively. Practice using tissues and disposing of them — it's a life skill that reduces germ spread.
Make sure your child gets enough outdoor time. Natural sunlight supports vitamin D production, mood regulation, and healthy sleep cycles.
If your child grinds their teeth at night, mention it at your next dental visit. It's usually harmless but worth monitoring.
Stay up to date on the annual flu vaccine. Children in group care settings are especially vulnerable during flu season.
Your child can handle more complex construction projects now. Building with interlocking bricks or blocks following simple instructions develops spatial reasoning and patience.
Introduce simple card games like "Go Fish" or matching games. They teach number recognition, strategy, and social skills all at once.

Outdoor play is essential — climbing, running, and swinging develop strength, coordination, and risk assessment. Preschoolers benefit from being active throughout the day, so aim for plenty of movement.
Your child may enjoy putting on "shows" or puppet performances. This dramatic play builds confidence, language skills, and emotional expression.
Simple science experiments — mixing baking soda and vinegar, growing seeds, or exploring magnets — spark curiosity and teach cause and effect.
Encourage your child to draw or paint their feelings. Art is a powerful outlet for emotions they may not yet have words for.
Your child is ready for games with simple rules like Simon Says or Red Light Green Light. These build listening skills and impulse control.
Playing with measuring cups, spoons, and water teaches early math concepts like volume, more/less, and estimation in a hands-on way.
Your child may enjoy creating with recycled materials — cardboard tubes, egg cartons, bottle caps. This open-ended play sparks creativity and resourcefulness.
Riding a balance bike or a bicycle with training wheels builds coordination and confidence that will transfer to riding without support later.
Play "I Spy" during car rides or walks. It sharpens observation skills and vocabulary while keeping your child engaged.
Planting seeds and watching them grow teaches patience, responsibility, and basic science. Let your child water their plant daily.
Lacing cards and bead-stringing activities build the fine motor precision your child will need for writing. Make it fun with colorful materials.
Create a treasure map of your backyard or home. Following a map introduces spatial concepts like left, right, near, and far.
Cooperative games where everyone works toward a shared goal teach teamwork and reduce the stress of competition for children still learning to lose gracefully.
Keep your child in a forward-facing car seat with a harness for as long as possible, up to the seat's maximum height and weight limits. Most children this age have not yet outgrown the harness.
Teach your child to always ask an adult before going near water. Even children who can swim should never be in or near water without supervision.
Practice what to do if your child gets separated from you in a store: stay where they are, look for a store worker, and never leave the building.
Your child can start learning their home address. Practice it regularly like a song or rhyme to help it stick.
Teach your child the concept of "safe adults" — parents, teachers, police officers — who they can go to for help. Avoid the vague term "stranger danger."
Your child should always wear a helmet for biking, scootering, and skating. Let them help choose one they like so they're more willing to wear it.
Kitchen safety awareness grows at this age. Teach your child that the stove, oven, and sharp objects are for adults, and model safe kitchen behavior.
Make sure your child knows not to open the front door without an adult present. A high deadbolt or chain lock adds a physical barrier.
Review playground rules: go down slides feet-first, wait your turn on the swings, and keep a safe distance from children who are swinging.
If your child uses a tablet or device, set up parental controls and keep screens in shared spaces. Teach them never to share personal information online.
Teach your child about body safety using proper anatomical names. Kids who know the correct words are better able to communicate if something is wrong.
Your child is old enough to practice calling emergency services on a phone and knowing what to say: their name, that they need help, and their address.
Garage doors, power tools, and workshop areas should always be off-limits without adult supervision. Use locks or alarms if needed.
When riding in the car, your child should always be in the back seat. The back seat is the safest spot for all children under 13.
Teach your child to stop at the edge of every driveway and sidewalk. Practice looking left, right, then left again before crossing together.
